cards.front: Where do pain and temperature fibres end in the spinal cord, compared with muscle afferents?
cards.back: Pain and temperature fibres stop in the dorsal horn; muscle afferents reach motor neurons in the ventral horn.
cards.quote: Pain and temperature fibres stop in the dorsal horn. Muscle afferents run on into the ventral horn to reach the motor neurons.

cards.front: Why can two growth cones exposed to the same guidance cue respond differently?
cards.back: Their receptors determine whether they detect and signal the cue; their internal signalling state helps determine whether the response is attraction or repulsion.
cards.quote: The cue marks the place; the growth cone decides what it means.
cards.section: The puzzle in the spinal cord

cards.front: The filopodia and lamellipodia of an axonal growth cone contain {{c1::actin}}.
cards.quote: a fan of actin-filled filopodia and lamellipodia at the axon's tip.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: How can repulsive cues help guide an axon along a path?
cards.back: They exclude the axon from neighbouring territories, channelling it between them. Other cues tell it where to stop.
cards.quote: Repellents fence off wrong territories, so an axon growing between them is channelled along its path, though other cues tell it where to stop.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: A cue makes actin fall apart on the left side of an axonal growth cone while actin builds on the right. Which way should it turn, and why?
cards.back: Rightward: growth cones turn toward the side where actin builds and away from the side where it falls apart.
cards.quote: It turns toward the side where actin builds and away from the side where actin falls apart.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: Brain membranes collapse cultured sensory growth cones. Liver and fibroblast membranes do not. What alternative explanation does this control weaken?
cards.back: It weakens the claim that any membrane preparation causes collapse; the activity depends on the tissue source.
cards.quote: membranes from liver or fibroblasts did not cause collapse, so collapse was not a response to any membrane at all.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: A brain preparation collapses sensory growth cones, but its activity disappears after heat or trypsin treatment. What kind of active substance does this support?
cards.back: A protein: both treatments destroy the collapse-inducing activity by damaging proteins.
cards.quote: the activity was destroyed by heat and by trypsin, so it was a protein.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: What visible change defines growth-cone collapse?
cards.back: The spread fan folds into a thin tip.
cards.quote: Within minutes the growth cones collapsed, folding from a spread fan into a thin tip.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: How does secretion versus membrane attachment change the range of a repulsive guidance cue?
cards.back: A secreted cue can repel from a distance; a membrane-bound cue acts through contact.
cards.quote: Some are secreted and repel from a distance; others sit in cell membranes and repel on contact.
cards.section: A growth cone that folds up

cards.front: The vertebrate guidance protein originally called collapsin is now called {{c1::Sema3A}}.
cards.quote: Collapsin is now Sema3A, the semaphorin this lesson follows.

cards.front: Why did the failure of chick retinal growth cones to collapse not show that purified collapsin was inactive?
cards.back: Sensory growth cones responded while retinal growth cones did not. An active cue can affect different growth cones differently.
cards.quote: Retinal growth cones did not respond to it: the cue was present, but those growth cones did not hear it.

cards.front: How are vertebrate semaphorin classes 3, 4–6 and 7 held or released?
cards.back: Class 3 is secreted; classes 4–6 span the membrane; class 7 is held by a lipid anchor.
cards.quote: The vertebrate classes differ in how the protein is held:

cards.front: Where is Sema3A made in the spinal cord to help exclude pain fibres?
cards.back: In the ventral cord.
cards.quote: Back to the spinal cord, where Sema3A is made in the ventral cord.

cards.front: At the stages tested, why can NT-3-supported muscle afferents enter ventral cord territory that excludes NGF-supported pain fibres?
cards.back: NGF-supported axons respond strongly to Sema3A repulsion; NT-3-supported axons respond weakly. Weak responsiveness does not establish attraction.
cards.quote: At this stage the NGF-dependent class responds to Sema3A, through a neuropilin-plexin receptor, and the NT-3-dependent class mostly does not, so only the first is kept out.

cards.front: NGF-supported sensory axons grow asymmetrically beside a ventral cord explant. If an antibody effectively blocks Sema3A, what should happen to the halo, and why?
cards.back: It should become more symmetric, because blocking Sema3A reduces the selective inhibition of axons facing the cord.
cards.quote: To test the idea, add an antibody against neuropilin-1 or against Sema3A: the NGF halo should become more symmetric.

cards.front: In hypothetical axon cultures, near/far lengths beside a source are 150/600 micrometres in A and 540/600 micrometres in B. Control ratios are near 1.0. Calculate each near-to-far ratio and identify the stronger asymmetry.
cards.back: A: 150/600 = 0.25. B: 540/600 = 0.90. A has the stronger asymmetry: relatively less growth faces the source.
cards.quote: Measure the axons on the side facing the source and on the far side.

cards.front: Why does a near-to-far axon-length ratio well below 1 not by itself prove repulsive turning?
cards.back: It shows less growth toward the source. A diffusible repellent or local growth inhibitor could cause that; control lengths and turning assays distinguish them.
cards.quote: A ratio well below 1 means the near side grew less, as a diffusible repellent or a local growth inhibitor would cause.

cards.front: Ventral cord tissue and cells secreting only Sema3A both suppress near-side growth in NGF-supported explants. Does this establish that Sema3A alone explains sensory sorting in vivo?
cards.back: No. The cells show Sema3A can produce the effect in culture; the tissue tests all released cues. Rule: a shared explant phenotype does not establish an exclusive cause in vivo, where other cues probably contribute.
cards.quote: A ventral cord explant tests everything the cord releases. Cells secreting Sema3A test Sema3A alone.

cards.front: In the usual Sema3A receptor pair, what jobs do neuropilin and plexin perform?
cards.back: Neuropilin catches the cue; plexin transmits the signal into the cell.
cards.quote: Neuropilin catches; plexin signals. That is the first part of the lesson's rule:

cards.front: Why can engineered cells bind Sema3A through neuropilin-1 alone yet fail to respond?
cards.back: Binding and signalling are separate jobs. Neuropilin catches Sema3A, but a plexin provides the intracellular signalling machinery.
cards.quote: A receptor has two jobs: catch the signal and pass it on.

cards.front: A sensory neuron retains working plexin but has neuropilin lacking its intracellular tail. Should that deletion necessarily abolish Sema3A-induced collapse, and why?
cards.back: No; collapse can persist. The experiments separate the jobs: neuropilin's tail is dispensable, whereas plexin's intracellular part is required.
cards.quote: Taken with the row above it, the result splits the jobs: neuropilin's tail is not needed, and the plexin's inner part is.

cards.front: How can adding a defective receptor protein block signalling even when the normal protein remains present?
cards.back: It can interfere with working receptor complexes: a dominant-negative effect. The blocking result alone need not reveal the exact interference mechanism.
cards.quote: A mutant that blocks the normal protein in this way is called a dominant negative.

cards.front: After expression of a receptor missing its intracellular region, a neuron stops turning to cue A but still turns toward cue B. What does the cue-B control show?
cards.back: The neuron retains the ability to turn. The result supports a defect in cue-A signalling rather than a general loss of turning ability.
cards.quote: The broken plexin interferes with the cell's own working receptor complexes.

cards.front: A GAP switches a small GTPase off by speeding {{c1::GTP hydrolysis}}.
cards.quote: a protein that speeds GTP hydrolysis and so switches a small GTPase off

cards.front: How can plexin GAP activity reduce a growth cone's adhesion to its substrate?
cards.back: It switches off a Ras-family GTPase reported as R-Ras or Rap. Both help maintain integrin adhesions, so switching either off lowers adhesion.
cards.quote: both help hold integrin adhesions to the substrate, so switching either off lowers adhesion.

cards.front: In sensory growth cones repelled by Sema3A, why can one-sided exposure cause turning and a sufficiently high uniform bath cause collapse?
cards.back: One-sided loosening biases the cone away from the source; loosening all sides can fold up the fan. Dose, exposure time and preparation also matter.
cards.quote: All round, a high enough dose can loosen every side, and in sensory growth cones the fan folds up: collapse.

cards.front: A sensory growth cone does not collapse in a low, uniform Sema3A bath. Must this contradict its turning away from a Sema3A pipette, and why?
cards.back: No. Collapse requires a sufficient dose in a suitable preparation, and depends on exposure time. Repulsive turning does not imply collapse at every uniform concentration.
cards.quote: dose, exposure time and the preparation matter as well as layout.

cards.front: Using f = c/(c + Kd), compare occupancy at c = 0.2 nM for illustrative Sema3A receptors: neuropilin alone, Kd = 1.0 nM; neuropilin–plexin, Kd = 0.2 nM. Which is more occupied?
cards.back: Alone: 0.2/(0.2 + 1.0) ≈ 0.17. Pair: 0.2/(0.2 + 0.2) = 0.50. The pair has about three times the occupancy; occupancy alone does not establish signalling.
cards.quote: 0.2 nM for the neuropilin-plexin pair and 1.0 nM for neuropilin alone

cards.front: For the illustrative neuropilin–plexin Kd of 0.2 nM, Sema3A is 0.21 nM near and 0.19 nM far. Using f = c/(c + Kd), calculate near and far occupancy and their difference in percentage points.
cards.quote: The near side is about 2.5 percentage points more occupied: a signal on one side.

cards.front: With Kd = 0.2 nM and f = c/(c + Kd), compare Sema3A occupancy contrasts for near/far concentrations of 52.5/47.5 nM versus 0.21/0.19 nM. How much smaller is the high-dose contrast, and does this prove collapse?
cards.back: High contrast: (52.5/52.7 − 47.5/47.7) × 100 ≈ 0.04 percentage points. Low: (0.21/0.41 − 0.19/0.39) × 100 ≈ 2.5 points, about sixty times larger. No: near-saturation compresses occupancy differences, but occupancy alone cannot predict collapse.
cards.quote: Almost every receptor is occupied, so even a gradient looks nearly uniform.

cards.front: Why can a simple Sema3A receptor-occupancy calculation not determine whether a growth cone turns or collapses?
cards.back: It describes binding, not the coupling to behaviour, and ignores amplification, adaptation and averaging over time.
cards.quote: The sketch describes receptor occupancy, not behaviour: it cannot predict a turn or a collapse, and it ignores amplification, adaptation and averaging over time.

cards.front: After a Xenopus spinal growth cone turns away from Sema3A, its cGMP pathway is activated and the same gradient conditions are reapplied. What happens, and why?
cards.back: It turns toward Sema3A. Activating the cGMP pathway changes how the growth cone interprets the cue, converting repulsion into attraction.
cards.quote: It turns toward Sema3A: with the cyclic GMP pathway activated, the same growth cones were attracted.

cards.front: The second messenger cGMP is made by {{c1::guanylate cyclases}}.
cards.quote: The senses and cGMP lesson introduced cGMP as a second messenger made by guanylate cyclases.

cards.front: What compartment-specific mechanism helps Sema3A attract an apical dendrite while repelling the same cortical neuron's axon?
cards.back: Soluble guanylate cyclase is concentrated mainly in the developing apical dendrite. Its production of cGMP is needed for dendritic attraction.
cards.quote: Soluble guanylate cyclase, an enzyme that makes cGMP, sits mainly in the developing apical dendrite and is needed for that attraction:

cards.front: Suppose raising cGMP in a cortical axon flips its Sema3A response as in the Xenopus turning assay. With Sema3A highest near the pial surface, which way should that axon grow, and why?
cards.back: Toward the pial surface, under that assumption. Rule: cGMP can reverse the sign of Sema3A guidance; the cortical gradient is highest near the surface, so an attracted axon would grow toward it.
cards.quote: In the developing cortex, Sema3A is high near the pial surface, the brain's outer surface.

cards.front: An axon explant has a symmetric halo beside a candidate repellent. Design measurements that distinguish absent response from inhibition on both sides and test directional repulsion.
cards.back: Compare absolute axon lengths and collapse with matched controls, and measure turning in a directional assay. Rule: a near-to-far ratio hides equal inhibition on both sides, while turning measures direction. Symmetry alone cannot diagnose signalling failure.
cards.quote: a symmetric halo alone cannot tell weak signalling from growth inhibited equally on both sides

cards.front: Age-matched NT-3-supported sensory growth cones have little of one neuropilin–plexin receptor component and weak Sema3A responses. How would you test whether low receptor abundance is causal?
cards.back: Restore the low component with expression controls; compare absolute growth, asymmetry and turning beside Sema3A versus control sources. Recovered avoidance supports receptor limitation. Rule: the receptor pair is necessary but does not guarantee a strong response, so failed rescue leaves other explanations open.
cards.quote: If a part is missing or low, express it in the NT-3-supported neurons, with controls for the expression itself, and repeat the explant test.

cards.front: What large shared region characterizes the semaphorin family?
cards.back: The sema domain.
cards.quote: all sharing one large region now called the sema domain.
cards.section: Fasciclin IV and the semaphorin family, in detail

cards.front: A cell has working Plexin-D1 signalling. If neuropilin is blocked, must the cell lose its Sema3E response, and why?
cards.back: No. Sema3E can bind Plexin-D1 without neuropilin, so blocking neuropilin need not interrupt this receptor route.
cards.quote: There are exceptions to the neuropilin route: Sema3E binds Plexin-D1 without neuropilin.
cards.section: How the receptor is switched on

cards.front: Two culture supplements select different sensory neuron populations and may also alter guidance sensitivity. How would you reduce this confounding when comparing their cue responses?
cards.back: Compare the populations in the same medium where possible and at matched ages; repeat across ages. Rule: a supplement can change both which neurons grow and how they respond, while sensitivity can change with maturation.
cards.quote: the NGF and NT-3 explant contrast mixes which neurons grow with how they respond.
cards.section: What the explant contrast mixes together
